title: Gateway API
text:
dc = DiscordClient()
gid = '1493461895615873044'
ch = await dc.channel('1493461896139903028')

The Gateway is Discord’s websocket for real-time events. The REST API answers requests. The Gateway pushes new messages, reactions, member joins, and other events as they happen.
The connection lifecycle:

Fetch the websocket URL from /gateway/bot.
Connect.
Receive Hello with the heartbeat interval.
Start the heartbeat loop.
Send Identify with the token and intents.
Receive Ready.

Intents tell Discord which events to send. They are bit flags combined with |. Intent names the full set from the gateway docs. GUILD_MEMBERS, GUILD_PRESENCES, and MESSAGE_CONTENT are privileged and must also be enabled in the Developer Portal.


source

Intent
def Intent(
    *args, **kwds
):
Gateway intents: OR members together and pass to GatewayClient



intents = Intent.GUILDS | Intent.GUILD_VOICE_STATES | Intent.GUILD_MESSAGES | Intent.MESSAGE_CONTENT
intents

<Intent.GUILDS|GUILD_VOICE_STATES|GUILD_MESSAGES|MESSAGE_CONTENT: 33409>


GatewayClient holds one gateway connection. It fetches the websocket URL from /gateway/bot when constructed, and dispatches each event to the handler registered for its type with on.


source

GatewayClient
def GatewayClient(
    intents, client, token:NoneType=None
):



gc = GatewayClient(intents, dc)
gc

GatewayClient(self.intents=<Intent.GUILDS|GUILD_VOICE_STATES|GUILD_MESSAGES|MESSAGE_CONTENT: 33409>, self.url='wss://gateway.discord.gg?v=10&encoding=json')


Op builds gateway payloads. Discord expects JSON with an op field (operation code) and a d field (data). Op.identify() and Op.heartbeat() return payloads ready to send.


source

Op
def Op(
    *args, **kwargs
):
dict subclass that also provides access to keys as attrs, and has a pretty markdown repr


A gateway event is JSON with four fields. op is the operation code: 0 dispatch, 1 heartbeat request, 10 hello, 11 heartbeat ACK. t is the event type name, such as MESSAGE_CREATE, present only on dispatches. s is the sequence number, present only on dispatches. Heartbeats and resumes send it back. d is the payload.
The client tracks the latest s. Event wraps the JSON and converts known dispatch types to their wrapper classes through evt_typs.

    msg, **kw
):

recv_evt reads one websocket message, wraps it as an Event, and updates the sequence counter. Call it directly to pull events one at a time when debugging.


source

GatewayClient.recv_evt
async def recv_evt():


gc.on registers the READY handler like any other dispatch handler. on_rdy stores session_id, user_id, and resume_gateway_url, the three values a Resume needs. Discord returns resume_gateway_url bare. The client appends the same version and encoding query as the initial connection, as the docs require.


source

GatewayClient.on
def on(
    event_type, handler
):


The gateway runs two loops. _hb sends heartbeats at the interval Discord specifies and watches for ACKs. A missed ACK means the connection is dead. _hb closes it with code 4000. That code keeps the session valid for a Resume. _listen reads events and dispatches them by opcode. On disconnect it calls _reconnect to open a fresh websocket. The new connection sends Hello (op 10). The Hello handler restarts the heartbeat and sends Identify on a first connect or Resume when a session exists. Op 7 (Reconnect) takes the same path.
All reconnection goes through _reconnect. A resume closes with code 4000 and opens a socket to resume_gateway_url. A re-identify closes with 1000 and returns to the original gateway URL. Code 1000 invalidates the session. The Hello handler then takes over.
start opens the websocket and starts the listener. The listener handles Hello, starts the heartbeat, and sends Identify. Events drive the whole connection lifecycle.

    debug:bool=False
):

Let’s now test that our gateway is getting events. Here is a simple handlers for new messages.

async def on_msg(msg):
    if msg.get('guild_id') != gid: return
    if not msg.author.get('bot'): return
    print(f"{msg.author['username']}: {msg.content}")

gc.on('MESSAGE_CREATE', on_msg)

The handler prints a message sent to the channel.

await ch.send('Test our event listener! Otters are awesome 🦦')

Message(id=1544802822153969789, author='DBuddy', content='Test our event listener! Otter…')


Next, a reconnect that resumes and one that re-identifies. The handler should still print after each.

await gc._reconnect(resume=True)
await asyncio.sleep(2)
await ch.send('Houston, do we have a problem?')

Message(id=1544802837282689168, author='DBuddy', content='Houston, do we have a problem?')



await gc._reconnect(resume=False)
await asyncio.sleep(2)
await ch.send('Did we re-identify?')

Message(id=1544802851937722498, author='DBuddy', content='Did we re-identify?')


Those reconnects were polite ones the client started. A real disconnect arrives as ConnectionClosed in the listener. The listener classifies the close code per the docs. Transient codes resume. 4007 and 4009 re-identify. 4004 and 4010 to 4014 (bad token, bad shard, bad intents) stop. Closing the live socket with a non-1000 code triggers the transient path. The heartbeat watchdog does the same on a dead connection. The listener should resume without help.

await gc.ws.close(code=4000)
await asyncio.sleep(3)
await ch.send('Back from the dead? (listener auto-resume)')

Message(id=1544802865732657222, author='DBuddy', content='Back from the dead? (listener …')


Identifying with a corrupted token gets close code 4004. The client must stop instead of retrying.

gc_bad = GatewayClient(intents, dc)
gc_bad.token = gc_bad.token[:-4] + 'zzzz'
await gc_bad.start()
for _ in range(30):
    if not gc_bad.running: break
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
assert not gc_bad.running

gateway closed: 4004 Authentication failed.


stop cancels both background tasks and closes the websocket with code 1000. That tells Discord to invalidate the session. A later start identifies from scratch.


source

GatewayClient.stop
async def stop():



await gc.stop()

title: cordslite API
text:
from fastcore.test import *
import tempfile
Discord has three APIs. The REST API handles actions such as sending a message, listing channels, or fetching history. The Gateway API pushes real-time events over a websocket. The Voice API streams audio over UDP.
The REST API needs a bot token from the Discord Developer Portal:
DiscordClient wraps an httpx2 client with Discord’s base URL (https://discord.com/api/v10) and the auth header set.
source

DiscordClient
def DiscordClient(
    token:NoneType=None, # Bot token, defaulting to `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN`
    user_token:NoneType=None, # User token, defaulting to `DISCORD_USER_TOKEN`. Used by `use_user=True` calls, and by every call when there is no bot token
    name:str='cordslite', # Client name for the User-Agent header
    ver:str='0.1', # Client version for the User-Agent header
):
Async client for Discord’s REST API
DiscordClient reads DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN from the environment when it gets no token. Tokens are stripped of surrounding whitespace, since a pasted token often carries a trailing newline, and a blank token counts as absent.
dc = DiscordClient()
pasted = DiscordClient(token=' abc\n', user_token='\txyz ')
test_eq((pasted.token, pasted.user_token), ('abc', 'xyz'))
test_is(DiscordClient(token='x', user_token=' \n').user_token, None)

Every REST call goes through _req. On 429 Too Many Requests it waits for Retry-After seconds and retries. Any other non-2xx response raises DiscordError with Discord’s error code, message, and HTTP status.

Discord’s REST endpoints return JSON with many fields. DiscordObject wraps the raw dict instead of declaring a property per field. Fields read as obj.name or obj['name']. __dir__ lists them for tab completion in notebooks. New fields Discord adds are available without a code change.

A DM is an ordinary channel in Discord’s API. create_dm posts to /users/@me/channels with a recipient_id and returns a standard Channel. send and messages work on it unchanged. In gateway events a DM message has no guild_id. A handler can tell DMs from guild messages by that missing field.

Reading a person’s own DMs needs that person’s account token, not a bot’s. DiscordClient reads DISCORD_USER_TOKEN from the environment, or takes user_token. With no bot token it authenticates every request as the user. With both, a call passes use_user=True to send the user token for that request. Discord’s terms forbid automating a user account, so keep this to reading your own messages, and expect the token to change when the password does.
dms lists the account’s open DM channels from /users/@me/channels, which is empty for a bot. A DM (type 1) has no name and one recipient. A group DM (type 3) can have a name and several.

Voice uses three connections at once. The main gateway websocket (gc) requests the join and receives the voice server details. A second websocket to the voice server coordinates the session. A UDP connection carries the audio. Audio goes over UDP because low latency matters more than guaranteed delivery. VoiceClient owns the voice websocket and the UDP connection for one channel. The voice heartbeat differs from the main gateway’s. Protocol v8 requires seq_ack, the sequence number of the last message from the server. The heartbeat must start as soon as Hello arrives, before UDP setup. Otherwise the voice server closes the websocket with code 4006.

Op 13 (CLIENT_DISCONNECT) reports that a user left the channel. The client drops that user’s decoder and SSRC mapping. Without this, a user who rejoins inherits stale jitter state. The maps also grow for the length of the session.

The voice gateway runs two loops. _hb sends heartbeats at the interval Discord specifies and watches for ACKs. A missed ACK closes the socket with code 4000. That code preserves the session for a resume. _reconnect handles both resume and fresh reconnect. A resume keeps session_id, token, endpoint, the UDP socket, and the DAVE state. A fresh reconnect resets the audio session and re-runs _join for new server details. _listen schedules _reconnect as its own task. _reconnect therefore cancels _listen_task only when called from elsewhere. A reconnect that cancelled the task it runs in would kill itself. Failed attempts retry with exponential backoff, capped at 30 seconds. The counter resets once the client establishes or resumes a session. Recording state survives both paths. Per-user files keep accumulating across a reconnect, with a silence gap during the swap.

VoiceClient.reset_audio
def reset_audio():


_listen runs the voice gateway state machine. On HELLO (op 8) it sends voice_resume if self.resuming holds and voice_identify otherwise. Op 9 confirms the resume at the gateway level. Media encryption is a separate handshake. DAVE must catch up before outgoing audio can be encrypted again. The client waits on _wait_dave_ready before setting resumed.
When the socket closes, the close code decides the recovery (docs). Codes 4003 to 4006, 4009, and 4011 mean the session’s credentials are dead. The main gateway issues voice tokens per session. The client rejoins from scratch to get fresh ones. A resume with dead credentials loops. Live testing showed that a bad resume gets 4003 Not authenticated, not 4006. Code 4014 means an admin kicked or moved the bot, or Discord is swapping the voice server. The client must not reconnect to that endpoint. It waits for gateway events instead. Any other code, such as 4015 (voice server crashed), is transient. The client resumes. Recovery runs as a separate task. The dying listener never cancels its own reconnect. The listener logs handler errors and skips them. They do not stop it.

Audio arrives as RTP packets over UDP. Each packet has a 12-byte or longer RTP header, an encrypted payload, and a 4-byte nonce at the end. The header carries the sequence number, the timestamp, and the SSRC that identifies the speaker. The payload is Opus audio wrapped by DAVE, then encrypted with Discord’s transport key secret_key.
Decryption has two stages. The transport layer uses aead_xchacha20_poly1305_rtpsize. The cipher takes a 24-byte nonce. Only 4 bytes travel in the packet. The client pads them with 20 zero bytes. The plain RTP header is the AAD: authenticated, not encrypted. In rtpsize mode the AAD covers the 12-byte base header, any CSRC entries, and the 4-byte extension preamble only. The extension data itself is inside the encrypted payload. Its length is in the preamble, as a count of 32-bit words. Packets without the extension bit have no extension data. The frame that remains is DAVE-protected. self.dave.decrypt unwraps it using the user id from the SSRC map. Voice SPEAKING events fill that map. The result is the Opus payload.
A packet whose second byte is 0x78 is RTP voice data. Other values, such as 0xC9, are RTCP control packets for quality reporting. The client skips them.

VoiceClient.decrypt
def decrypt(
    pkt, uid

An earlier version skipped a fixed 8 bytes of extension. It corrupted audio whenever the extension was not two words. On packets with no extension it discarded real Opus data. Discord offers no way to request a particular extension size. The cell below builds RTP packets by hand and runs them through the real cipher: extensions of 0, 2, and 3 words, no extension, and no DAVE session. Without DAVE the transport plaintext is the Opus frame.

_key = bytes(range(32))
def _mk_pkt(payload, ext_words=2, has_ext=True):
    hdr = struct.pack('>BBHII', 0x80 | (0x10 if has_ext else 0), 0x78, 1, 960, 1234)
    if has_ext: hdr += struct.pack('>HH', 0xBEDE, ext_words)
    n4 = (7).to_bytes(4, 'big')
    enc = xchacha_encrypt((bytes(4 * ext_words) if has_ext else b'') + payload, hdr, n4 + b'\0'*20, _key)
    return hdr + enc + n4


fvc = object.__new__(VoiceClient)
fvc.secret_key = _key
cases = [dict(ext_words=0), dict(ext_words=2), dict(ext_words=3), dict(has_ext=False)]
test_eq([fvc.decrypt(_mk_pkt(b'opus!', **kw), 0) for kw in cases], [b'opus!']*len(cases))

decode turns RTP voice packets into PCM and keeps each speaker’s stream in order without a jitter buffer. It compares RTP sequence numbers modulo 16 bits. It accepts wraparound from 65535 to 0. It drops duplicates and packets behind the last accepted sequence. A forward gap means packet loss. Small gaps use Opus packet-loss concealment. Larger gaps use silence.
decode decrypts and decodes a packet before its sequence and timestamp become accepted state. A corrupt packet cannot move the stream backwards or poison the next gap calculation. decode discards a reordered packet rather than buffering it. Recording stays simple at the cost of an occasional 20 ms loss.

Recording opens one ffmpeg process per speaker and writes that speaker’s decoded PCM to its stdin. Each file covers the whole session. _written counts the samples on disk per user. Before each write the track is padded with silence up to the current wall-clock position. Audio therefore sits at the moment the user spoke it, whether the user joined late, paused, or left and rejoined. Padding happens only when a track is more than 200 ms behind. While someone is speaking, each packet appends its 20 ms and the track keeps pace. Arrival jitter never inserts silence mid-sentence. A packet whose SSRC has had no Speaking event yet has no owner, and is dropped rather than recorded under the SSRC.
start_recording drains the UDP queue first. Stale packets from before the recording never reach the new files.
stop_recording pads every track with silence out to the stop time. All files are then session length and aligned. It closes each ffmpeg stdin and waits for the process. That finalizes the containers. Without it the files can look valid but lack the buffered audio at the end.

{'onset': 1.049, 'sent_at': 1.001, 'dur': 2.127, 'sess_len': 2.162}


The second bot leaves before the disconnect scenarios below, which concern this bot’s own connection.

await vcb.leave()
await gcb.stop()

DEBUG: Received Opcode: 0


The last case is an admin disconnecting the bot. Discord sends the bot’s own VOICE_STATE_UPDATE with a null channel and closes the voice socket with 4014. The client must tear down, finalize any recording in progress, and not rejoin. The cell does this to the bot over REST.

vc.start_recording('/tmp/kick_test.mp3')
await asyncio.sleep(1)
await vch('PATCH', f'/guilds/{gld.id}/members/{gc.user_id}', channel_id=None)
for _ in range(30):
    if not vc.running: break
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
assert not vc.running and not vc._recording

DEBUG: Received Opcode: 0
DEBUG: Received Opcode: 0
DEBUG: Received Opcode: 0
removed from voice channel; disconnecting


Recording can continue across reconnect types.

vc.start_recording()
await asyncio.sleep(2)
procs_before, start_before = dict(vc._rec_procs), vc._rec_start
await vc._reconnect(resume=False)
await asyncio.sleep(3)
await vc.stop_recording()

{'speakers': {}, 'mixed': None}



await vc.play_file("/tmp/recording_mixed.mp3")


await vc.leave()

title: cordslite 🍺
text:
How to use

Setup
Getting a bot token:

Go to the Discord Developer Portal.
Create an application, then add a bot under “Bot”.
Copy the token and set it as an environment variable:

export DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN='your_token_here'

Under “OAuth2”, generate an invite URL with the bot scope and the permissions you need, and open it to invite the bot to your server.

Then create the client:

from cordslite import *


dc = DiscordClient()



Guilds and Channels
Fetch a guild (server) and explore its channels:

gid = '1493461895615873044'
gld = await dc.guild(gid)

Gateway (Real-time Events)
Connect, then register handlers for events such as MESSAGE_CREATE:

intents = Intent.GUILDS | Intent.GUILD_VOICE_STATES | Intent.GUILD_MESSAGES | Intent.MESSAGE_CONTENT
gc = GatewayClient(intents, dc)
await gc.start()


async def on_msg(msg): print(f"{msg.author['username']}: {msg.content}")

gc.on('MESSAGE_CREATE', on_msg)

await gc.stop()



Bot
Bot ties REST and Gateway together with a decorator-based command router. It lives in cordslite.bot, alongside the voice support, and needs the voice extra: pip install cordslite[voice]. The function name becomes the command name, prefixed with ! in Discord:

from cordslite.bot import *


bot = Bot(intents)
await bot.start()


@bot.cmd
async def echo(msg, args): await (await msg.channel).send(f'You said: {args}')

bot

Bot(cmds=['echo'])


The router catches errors in command handlers and stores them in bot.errors. You can also register a handler that runs as they happen:

@bot.on_error
async def handle_err(msg, e): print(f'Error: {e}')

vc.start_recording(path='/tmp/recording.mp3')
